implementation_notes: The default C++ realization keeps both buffers in one contiguous pair and publishes an index: the writer fills `buffers[1 - current]` and publishes with `current.store(next, std::memory_order_release)`, while readers (any thread, or the next frame) load with `memory_order_acquire` and index the array. The swap is a single store regardless of buffer size, nothing is allocated after construction, and the two buffers stay adjacent - the form Nystrom's framebuffer example uses. Assume exactly one writer: several concurrent publishers must go through the atomic shared_ptr variant or a lock, because a lost index update silently drops a frame.
pitfalls: Single-writer assumption: two threads publishing concurrently overwrite each other's index update - serialize the swap or use compare_exchange.
Loading the index relaxed on the reader side and then reading the buffer is a data race; the reader's load must be acquire.
Buffers must be fully constructed before the first publish and never resized afterwards - the index re-points, it never moves storage.

variants.name: std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<const T>> publication
variants.implementation_notes: When frames outlive a pass - readers on other threads, deferred consumers, resources that must stay alive until every reader is done - own them with `std::shared_ptr` and swap through the C++20 specialization `std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<const Buffer>>`: `store` atomically replaces the pointer and the associated use_count update is part of the atomic operation, while `load` returns a copy that keeps the old frame alive as long as the reader holds it. This removes the lifetime hazard of the raw-pointer pair at the price of an atomic shared_ptr, which is not guaranteed lock-free (check `is_lock_free()`). Pre-C++20 code used the free `std::atomic_*` functions on shared_ptr, deprecated in C++20.
pitfalls: `std::atomic<std::shared_ptr>` is not guaranteed lock-free: it may take a lock per load/store, so measure before putting it in a hot frame loop.
All non-const access to a shared_ptr must go through the atomic instance - mixing plain and atomic accesses to the same shared_ptr is a data race.
Readers that keep their copy delay reclamation of the old frame even though the swap itself was cheap.

variants.name: Mutex-guarded pair (portable pre-C++20 form)
variants.implementation_notes: When the buffer is a container pair and the swap is not a single store (or the toolchain predates C++20), guard the swap and the readers with a mutex: the writer finishes the back container, then `std::swap(current, next)` under `std::lock_guard`, and readers take the same lock long enough to copy the snapshot out. This is the simplest correct form and the right reach for application code that swaps rarely; it costs a coarse critical section and does not scale to many readers the way the atomic variants do.
pitfalls: Holding the lock while building the next buffer turns the swap into a long critical section; build outside, swap inside.
`std::shared_mutex` (C++17) readers can still starve a waiting writer; do not treat a reader lock as free.
Copying the snapshot out under the lock makes readers O(size) - only worth it when readers cannot tolerate a reference into the pair.
